title: Chock the diagonally opposite wheel and set the jack at the jacking point
instruction: Get the car ready to lift its front left wheel.
context: Automotive service technicians lift a corner of a car many times a day (O*NET 49-3023.00). Before lifting, they chock the wheel diagonally opposite the one coming up, in front and behind. That wheel stays loaded while the car tilts, so a chock there stops it rolling off the jack. The jack's saddle goes under the jacking point the maker marks on the sill, not under the floor pan, which it would dent. The instruction names neither rule. The car's nose has round headlights and a grille, and the car's own left (the driver's side in the US) faces the robot. Other tasks chock a cradle on both sides (#928) or jack a beam onto stands (#830). Here the robot must work out which wheel to chock from the one being lifted, and find the marked lifting point.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A fixed blue model hatchback, 16 cm wide, 36 cm long and 14.6 cm tall, stands on the bench centered at x 29.5, y 0, side-on to the robot. Its nose points to the robot's left (+y), so the car's left side faces the arms (x 21.5) and its right side is the far side (x 37.5). It has round headlights and a grille at the front, red tail lights at the back, and four black tires (5.8 cm across, 1.9 cm wide) on silver rims, centered at y +11.5 (front) and -11.5 (rear), x 22.5 (left) and 36.5 (right). The body's underside is 2.5 cm above the bench. Under each sill is a pinch-weld flange with a bright jacking-point patch 7 mm in from the sill's face, at y +6.1 and -6.1 on both sides, each with a small white triangle on the sill above it. A red trolley jack, 7 x 3.6 cm, 80 g, stands in front of the car's nose with its round saddle (1.8 cm across, top 2 cm above the bench) at x 26.5, y 24.5, aimed at +x, and its hydraulic unit (2.3 cm across, 3.4 cm tall) 4.3 cm behind the saddle. Two yellow rubber wheel chocks (wedges 2.6 x 2.5 x 1.5 cm, 40 g each, with a black handle post 1.8 cm across and 3.25 cm tall, 4.2 cm out from the wedge's center) stand behind the car's tail, wedge centers at x 33, y -27 (toe toward -y) and x 22, y -27 (toe toward +y), handles toward +x.
scoring: Scored at the end. The jack is set at a point when it stands upright (within 15 degrees), still, on the bench, with its saddle's center under that point's pinch-weld patch: within 5 mm across the sill and 1.5 cm along it. A chock is snug against a tire when it is upright and still on the bench, its wedge's center within 1.5 cm of the tire's center line across the car, its toe toward the tire and its center no more than 1 cm farther from the tire than touching. The score is 0 if the jack is under the car, upright or tipped over, other than set at the front left jacking point, or if a chock is against the front left tire. Otherwise it is 1.0 with the jack at the front left jacking point and the rear right tire chocked in front and behind; 0.5 with the jack there and one side of the rear right tire chocked, or both sides chocked without the jack; 0.25 with only the jack there or only one side chocked; 0 otherwise. Chocks at the other wheels count for nothing. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. In a real trial, check by eye and ruler which tire each chock touches, and look under the sill to see where the saddle is.
reset_notes: Stand the jack and both chocks back at their start positions. The car is fixed to the bench.
fidelity: The car is a fixed model at about 1:10. The jack and chocks are oversized for it so the grippers can hold them, and each chock has a long handle post so the gripper stays clear of the car's side. The jack isn't pumped: the task ends with the saddle under the point. Props are modeled shapes that collide as simple blocks; the tires collide as stacked slabs that follow their curve. Rigid-body physics only.
